items.concept_title: An introduction to the periodic table
items.prompt: Element A has an atomic number of 11, and Element B has an atomic number of 17. If these two elements were to form an ionic compound, which of the following best describes the resulting species and the reason for its formation?
items.helper_text: Determine the group number of each element first to see how many electrons they need to lose or gain.

options.label: A
options.text: A+ and B- are formed to achieve a stable octet configuration similar to noble gases.

options.label: B
options.text: A2+ and B2- are formed to minimize the total energy of the system.

options.label: C
options.text: A- and B+ are formed because Element A has a higher electronegativity.

options.label: D
options.text: A and B form a covalent bond because their electronegativity difference is small.

items.explanation: Element A (Na, Group 1) wants to lose 1 electron to reach a noble gas configuration (Na+). Element B (Cl, Group 17) wants to gain 1 electron to reach a noble gas configuration (Cl-). This transfer results in an ionic bond driven by the octet rule.

rubric.correct: The student correctly predicts the ions and the underlying reason (octet rule/stability).
common_misconceptions: Incorrectly assigning charges based on atomic number rather than valence electrons.
Confusing ionic bonding with covalent bonding for highly electropositive/electronegative pairs.

items.concept_title: An introduction to the periodic table
items.prompt: Consider the following set of elements: Mg (Z=12), Al (Z=13), and Si (Z=14). Based on their positions in the periodic table, which of the following correctly ranks them in order of increasing first ionization energy?
items.helper_text: Recall the periodic trend for ionization energy as you move from left to right across a period.

options.label: A
options.text: Mg < Al < Si

options.label: B
options.text: Si < Al < Mg

options.label: C
options.text: Al < Mg < Si

options.label: D
options.text: Mg < Si < Al

items.explanation: Across a period (from Mg to Si), the atomic number increases, meaning the effective nuclear charge (Zeff) increases. A higher Zeff pulls electrons more tightly, making them harder to remove. Therefore, ionization energy increases from left to right: Mg < Al < Si.

rubric.correct: The student correctly applies the periodic trend of increasing ionization energy across a period.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that increasing atomic number always leads to a simple linear increase without considering shell structure.
Reversing the trend (thinking ionization energy decreases across a period).

items.concept_title: An introduction to the periodic table
items.prompt: An element Y belongs to the d-block of the periodic table. It has the electron configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵. Which of the following is most likely true about element Y?
items.helper_text: Look at the subshell being filled; d-block elements are transition metals.

options.label: A
options.text: It is a highly reactive non-metal located in Period 4.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a transition metal with a partially filled d-subshell.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a noble gas because its d-subshell is half-filled.

options.label: D
options.text: It is an alkali metal because it has two electrons in the 4s orbital.

items.explanation: The presence of a partially filled d-subshell ([Ar] 4s² 3d⁵) is the defining characteristic of transition metals. Specifically, 3d⁵ represents Manganese (Mn), which is a transition metal.

rubric.correct: The student identifies the element as a transition metal based on its electron configuration.
common_misconceptions: Mistaking d-block elements for s-block elements due to the 4s² configuration.
Assuming half-filled shells imply noble gas stability (which applies to p-block octets, not d-blocks).

items.concept_title: An introduction to the periodic table
items.prompt: Element P is in Period 3, Group 2. Element Q is in Period 3, Group 17. If we compare the ionic radius of P⁺ and Q⁻, which statement is correct?
items.helper_text: Compare how losing an electron affects a cation versus how gaining an electron affects an anion.

options.label: A
options.text: P⁺ is larger than Q⁻ because it has more protons.

options.label: B
options.text: Q⁻ is larger than P⁺ because it has more electrons and higher electron-electron repulsion.

options.label: C
options.text: They are equal in size because they are in the same period.

options.label: D
options.text: P⁺ is larger because it has more electron shells than Q⁻.

items.explanation: P (Mg) forms P⁺ (Mg²⁺) by losing electrons, reducing electron-electron repulsion and losing a shell (if it were in a higher period, but here it just loses a shell's worth of effective volume). Q (Cl) forms Q⁻ (Cl⁻) by gaining an electron, which increases electron-electron repulsion within the same shell, causing the cloud to expand. Therefore, an anion (Q⁻) is significantly larger than a cation (P⁺) of the same period.

rubric.correct: The student correctly compares the sizes of a cation and an anion based on electron repulsion and shell dynamics.
common_misconceptions: Assuming cations are larger than anions.
Thinking that being in the same period makes ions of different types equal in size.

items.concept_title: An introduction to the periodic table
items.prompt: Which of the following sets of elements is ordered correctly from most metallic to most non-metallic?
items.helper_text: Remember: Metallic character increases as you go down and to the left of the periodic table.

options.label: A
options.text: Li, Na, K, Rb

options.label: B
options.text: F, Cl, Br, I

options.label: C
options.text: Cs, K, Na, Li

options.label: D
options.text: O, S, Se, Te

items.explanation: Metallic character increases down a group (as ionization energy decreases) and decreases across a period (as electronegativity increases). Cs is at the bottom of Group 1 (most metallic), while Li is at the top (least metallic in that group). Therefore, Cs > K > Na > Li represents a decrease in metallic character, or an increase in non-metallic character. Wait, the question asks for 'most metallic to most non-metallic'. Cs is the most metallic, Li is the least. So Cs -> Li is correct.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the trend of metallic character across a group.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the direction of the metallic trend with the electronegativity trend.
Selecting a group that is ordered in reverse (e.g., Group 17).

items.prompt:
A voltaic cell is constructed using a magnesium (Mg) electrode and a silver (Ag) electrode. The standard reduction potentials are given as follows:
E° (Mg²⁺/Mg) = -2.37 V
E° (Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V

Which of the following statements correctly describes the cell operation?
items.helper_text: Remember that the anode is where oxidation occurs (lower reduction potential) and E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode.

options.label: A
options.text: Silver acts as the anode and magnesium acts as the cathode.

options.label: B
options.text: Magnesium acts as the anode and the cell potential (E°cell) is +3.17 V.

options.label: C
options.text: Magnesium acts as the anode and the cell potential (E°cell) is -3.17 V.

options.label: D
options.text: Silver acts as the anode and the cell potential (E°cell) is +1.57 V.

items.explanation: In a voltaic cell, the electrode with the lower (more negative) reduction potential undergoes oxidation and acts as the anode. Here, Mg (-2.37 V) is lower than Ag (+0.80 V), so Mg is the anode. The cathode is Ag. The standard cell potential is calculated as: E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode = 0.80 V - (-2.37 V) = +3.17 V.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies magnesium as the anode due to its lower reduction potential and calculates a positive cell potential of 3.17 V.
common_misconceptions: Subtracting the values incorrectly (e.g., 0.80 - 2.37) resulting in a negative cell potential.
Confusing the anode and cathode by choosing the more positive potential as the anode.

items.prompt: A voltaic cell is constructed using a copper electrode in a CuSO4 solution and a silver electrode in an AgNO3 solution. If the standard reduction potential for Cu2+/Cu is +0.34 V and for Ag+/Ag is +0.80 V, what will be the direction of electron flow and the sign of the anode in this cell?
items.helper_text: Compare the reduction potentials; the lower value indicates the species that undergoes oxidation.

options.label: A
options.text: Electrons flow from Cu to Ag; Anode is Cu

options.label: B
options.text: Electrons flow from Ag to Cu; Anode is Ag

options.label: C
options.text: Electrons flow from Cu to Ag; Anode is Ag

options.label: D
options.text: Electrons flow from Ag to Cu; Anode is Cu

items.explanation: In a voltaic cell, the electrode with the lower reduction potential acts as the anode (oxidation). Since E°(Cu2+/Cu) = +0.34 V is lower than E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V, Cu is the anode and Ag is the cathode. Electrons flow from the anode (Cu) to the cathode (Ag) through the external circuit.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the anode based on the lower reduction potential and the direction of electron flow from anode to cathode.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the higher reduction potential is the anode.
Thinking electrons flow from cathode to anode.

items.prompt: Consider a voltaic cell consisting of a Zn electrode in ZnSO4 and a Pb electrode in Pb(NO3)2. If the cell potential is measured to be 0.13 V, which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the cell reaction?
items.helper_text: A positive E°cell in a voltaic cell always implies a spontaneous redox reaction.

options.label: A
options.text: Zn is oxidized and Pb is reduced.

options.label: B
options.text: Pb is oxidized and Zn is reduced.

options.label: C
options.text: Both Zn and Pb are oxidized.

options.label: D
options.text: The cell is non-spontaneous because the potential is low.

items.explanation: In a voltaic cell, the cell potential (E°cell) must be positive for a spontaneous reaction. A positive E°cell indicates that the species with the lower reduction potential (Zn) is being oxidized (anode) and the species with the higher reduction potential (Pb) is being reduced (cathode).

rubric.correct: The student recognizes that a positive cell potential defines the oxidation/reduction roles.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the sign of E°cell with the spontaneity of the reaction.
Reversing the oxidation and reduction processes.

items.prompt: A voltaic cell is set up with a Magnesium electrode in MgSO4 and a Tin electrode in SnSO4. If the concentration of Mg2+ ions is increased significantly while the concentration of Sn2+ ions is decreased, how will the cell potential (E) change according to the Nernst equation?
items.helper_text: Think about the reaction quotient (Q) and how concentration shifts affect the equilibrium position.

options.label: A
options.text: The cell potential will increase.

options.label: B
options.text: The cell potential will decrease.

options.label: C
options.text: The cell potential will remain unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: The cell will stop functioning immediately.

items.explanation: The cell reaction is Mg + Sn2+ -> Mg2+ + Sn. According to the Nernst equation, E = E° - (RT/nF) ln(Q), where Q = [Mg2+]/[Sn2+]. Increasing the product concentration ([Mg2+]) and decreasing the reactant concentration ([Sn2+]) increases the reaction quotient (Q). As Q increases, the term subtracted from E° increases, thus decreasing E.

rubric.correct: The student correctly applies the Nernst equation logic to the change in concentrations.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that increasing reactant concentration always increases potential regardless of which ion is which.
Confusing the effect of concentration on E with Le Chatelier's principle without considering the Nernst equation's mathematical structure.

items.prompt: In a standard voltaic cell involving the reaction: 2Al(s) + 3Fe2+(aq) -> 2Al3+(aq) + 3Fe(s), what is the mass change observed at the anode during the process?
items.helper_text: Identify which species is being oxidized and what happens to a solid metal when it becomes an ion.

options.label: A
options.text: The anode mass increases because Al3+ ions deposit on it.

options.label: B
options.text: The anode mass decreases because Al atoms are oxidized to Al3+ ions.

options.label: C
options.text: The anode mass remains constant as it is a solid electrode.

options.label: D
options.text: The anode mass increases because electrons are added to the Al atoms.

items.explanation: In the given reaction, Al is being oxidized (Al -> Al3+ + 3e-). Since Al is the species being oxidized, it serves as the anode. During oxidation, solid metal atoms lose electrons and enter the solution as aqueous ions, leading to a loss of mass from the electrode.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies the anode as the site of oxidation and the resulting mass loss.
common_misconceptions: Misidentifying the anode as the cathode.
Thinking that oxidation results in mass gain.

items.prompt: A student forgets to include a salt bridge in a voltaic cell containing a Zn/Zn2+ half-cell and a Cu/Cu2+ half-cell. What is the immediate consequence of this error?
items.helper_text: Consider what happens to the electrical charge in each beaker as electrons move.

options.label: A
options.text: The electrons will flow in the opposite direction.

options.label: B
options.text: The cell potential will double to compensate.

options.label: C
options.text: The current will stop flowing almost immediately due to charge buildup.

options.label: D
options.text: The Zn electrode will become the cathode.

items.explanation: The salt bridge is essential for maintaining electrical neutrality. Without it, as electrons flow from the anode to the cathode, a positive charge builds up in the anode compartment and a negative charge builds up in the cathode compartment. This charge imbalance creates an opposing potential that stops the flow of electrons almost instantly.

rubric.correct: The student understands the role of the salt bridge in maintaining charge neutrality.
common_misconceptions: Thinking the cell will still work but with lower voltage.
Thinking the salt bridge only provides ions for the reaction, not for charge balance.

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: An unknown white powder is analyzed in a laboratory. When a small amount is heated in a crucible, it turns brown and releases a pungent gas. When it is dissolved in water, the resulting solution turns red litmus paper blue. Which of the following statements best describes the observations?
items.helper_text: Distinguish between a change (the process) and a property (the ability to undergo change).

options.label: A
options.text: The heating process is a physical change, while the litmus test is a chemical property.

options.label: B
options.text: Both the heating and the litmus test observations involve chemical properties and chemical changes.

options.label: C
options.text: The color change during heating is a physical property, while the gas release is a chemical property.

options.label: D
options.text: The solubility in water is a chemical property, while the gas release is a physical property.

items.explanation: Heating causing a color change and gas release indicates a chemical change (decomposition). The ability to change the color of litmus paper (reactivity with acid/base) is a chemical property. Therefore, both observations involve chemical aspects.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that both the transformation of the substance and its reactivity are chemical in nature.
common_misconceptions: Confusing a physical property like solubility with a chemical property.
Thinking a color change is always a physical property.

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: A student is given two samples: Sample X is a block of pure copper, and Sample Y is a mixture of copper powder and iron filings. Which of the following experimental procedures would allow the student to distinguish between the two based on their properties?
items.helper_text: Look for a property that is present in one component of the mixture but absent in the pure substance.

options.label: A
options.text: Measuring the mass of both samples using a digital balance.

options.label: B
options.text: Observing the luster of the samples under bright light.

options.label: C
options.text: Passing a magnet over the samples to check for magnetic susceptibility.

options.label: D
options.text: Heating both samples to see if they melt at the same temperature.

items.explanation: Magnetism is an intensive physical property. Since Sample Y contains iron (a ferromagnetic material) and Sample X is pure copper (diamagnetic), the magnet will react to Sample Y but not Sample X, allowing for a clear distinction.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies magnetism as a physical property that differentiates the mixture from the pure metal.
common_misconceptions: Assuming mass (an extensive property) can distinguish them without knowing the volume.
Thinking melting point is a reliable way to distinguish a mixture if the components have similar melting points.

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: Consider the following processes: (1) Sublimation of dry ice, (2) The rusting of an iron nail, (3) Dissolving sugar in tea, and (4) The combustion of magnesium ribbon. How many of these processes represent a change in the chemical identity of the matter?
items.helper_text: Determine if new substances are formed in each process.
items.explanation: Process (1) is a phase change (physical). Process (2) is oxidation (chemical). Process (3) is a mixture formation/dissolution (physical). Process (4) is oxidation/combustion (chemical). Only (2) and (4) change the identity.

rubric.correct: The student correctly categorizes rusting and combustion as chemical changes.
common_misconceptions: Classifying dissolution as a chemical change because the sugar 'disappears'.
Classifying sublimation as a chemical change because the state changes drastically.

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: An element has a density of 19.3 g/cm³, a melting point of 1054 °C, and is highly unreactive with most acids. Which of the following is the most accurate classification of these descriptions?
items.helper_text: Ask yourself: 'Does measuring this property change the substance into something else?'

options.label: A
options.text: Density and melting point are chemical properties; unreactivity is a physical property.

options.label: B
options.text: Density and melting point are physical properties; unreactivity is a chemical property.

options.label: C
options.text: All three descriptions are physical properties of the element.

options.label: D
options.text: All three descriptions are chemical properties of the element.

items.explanation: Density and melting point can be measured without changing the substance's identity (physical). The ability (or lack thereof) to react with acid describes how the substance interacts to form new compounds (chemical).

rubric.correct: The student distinguishes between measurable physical constants and reactivity-based chemical properties.
common_misconceptions: Thinking that because 'reactivity' is a characteristic, it must be a physical property.
Confusing melting point (physical) with burning (chemical).

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: A sample of liquid A boils at 78 °C and is highly flammable. A sample of liquid B boils at 100 °C and is non-flammable. When analyzing these substances, a scientist notes that liquid A reacts violently with oxygen. Which statement correctly identifies the properties being discussed?
items.helper_text: Flammability involves the formation of new substances (like CO2 and H2O).

options.label: A
options.text: Boiling point is a chemical property, and flammability is a physical property.

options.label: B
options.text: Boiling point is a physical property, and flammability/reactivity with oxygen are chemical properties.

options.label: C
options.text: Both boiling point and flammability are physical properties because they are observed in the liquid state.

options.label: D
options.text: Both boiling point and flammability are chemical properties because they involve energy changes.

items.explanation: Boiling point is a physical property (phase change). Flammability and reactivity with oxygen describe the substance's ability to undergo a chemical reaction, making them chemical properties.

rubric.correct: The student correctly categorizes phase change properties as physical and reactivity properties as chemical.
common_misconceptions: Thinking flammability is physical because it is an 'observable' trait.
Thinking boiling point is chemical because it involves heat.

items.concept_title: Physical and chemical properties of matter
items.prompt: A researcher is trying to purify a sample of salt (NaCl) from a mixture of salt and sand. The researcher decides to add water, filter the mixture, and then evaporate the water. Which of the following is true regarding the properties used in this separation?
items.helper_text: Does dissolving salt in water create a new chemical compound, or just a mixture?

options.label: A
options.text: The separation relies on the chemical property of solubility and the physical property of boiling point.

options.label: B
options.text: The separation relies on the chemical property of solubility and the chemical property of boiling point.

options.label: C
options.text: The separation relies on the physical property of solubility and the physical property of boiling point.

options.label: D
options.text: The separation relies on the physical property of density and the physical property of boiling point.

items.explanation: Solubility (the ability to dissolve) is a physical property because no new substance is formed when salt dissolves in water; it remains NaCl in solution. Evaporation (boiling) is a physical phase change. Therefore, both are physical properties.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes that both solubility and boiling point are physical properties used in separation techniques.
common_misconceptions: Classifying solubility as a chemical property because it involves interaction with water.
Classifying evaporation as a chemical property because it involves heat.

items.prompt: In a chemical reaction between two gaseous reactants, a scientist observes that increasing the concentration of one reactant significantly increases the reaction rate. According to collision theory, which of the following best explains this observation?
items.helper_text: Think about how 'crowding' more people into a small room affects how often they bump into each other.

options.label: A
options.text: The increased concentration lowers the activation energy required for the reaction to occur.

options.label: B
options.text: The increased concentration increases the frequency of collisions between reactant particles.

options.label: C
options.text: The increased concentration increases the proportion of particles that possess kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The increased concentration increases the velocity of the individual reactant particles.

items.explanation: According to collision theory, for a reaction to occur, particles must collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation. Increasing the concentration means there are more particles in a given volume, which directly leads to a higher frequency of collisions per unit of time, thereby increasing the reaction rate. Option A refers to catalysts, Option C refers to temperature, and Option D is incorrect because concentration does not change individual particle velocity (which is temperature-dependent).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that concentration affects collision frequency.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the effect of concentration with the effect of temperature (energy distribution).
Confusing the effect of concentration with the effect of a catalyst (activation energy).

items.prompt: In a controlled chemical reaction between gas A and gas B, an increase in temperature from 300 K to 310 K results in a significant increase in the reaction rate. According to collision theory, which of the following best explains the primary reason for this rate enhancement?
items.helper_text: Consider whether the change in total collisions or the change in the energy of those collisions has a larger impact on the rate.

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of collisions per second increases due to higher kinetic energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The frequency of collisions increases, but the proportion of effective collisions increases more significantly.

options.label: C
options.text: The activation energy required for the reaction is lowered by the increased thermal energy.

options.label: D
options.text: The orientation of the molecules becomes more favorable as they move faster.

items.explanation: While an increase in temperature does increase the total collision frequency (A), the exponential increase in the number of molecules possessing kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy (Ea) is the dominant factor. Therefore, the increase in the fraction of 'effective' collisions is the primary driver of the rate increase.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that the increase in the fraction of molecules exceeding activation energy is the dominant factor.
common_misconceptions: Believing that temperature primarily works by increasing the total number of collisions.
Confusing temperature increase with a decrease in activation energy.

items.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reaction where the rate-determining step involves the breaking of a strong covalent bond. How does the catalyst specifically influence the collision theory parameters to increase the reaction rate?
items.helper_text: Think about how the 'energy barrier' changes when a catalyst is introduced.

options.label: A
options.text: It increases the collision frequency by providing a surface for molecules to cluster.

options.label: B
options.text: It increases the average kinetic energy of the reactants, allowing more collisions to be successful.

options.label: C
options.text: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the frequency of effective collisions.

options.label: D
options.text: It aligns the reactant molecules into a more favorable orientation before they collide.

items.explanation: A catalyst does not change the kinetic energy (temperature) or the total number of collisions significantly; instead, it changes the mechanism (pathway) to one with a lower activation energy. This means a much larger fraction of existing collisions now meet the energy requirement to be 'effective'.

rubric.correct: The student correctly links the catalyst to a lower activation energy and an increase in effective collisions.
common_misconceptions: Thinking catalysts increase the temperature or kinetic energy of the system.
Thinking catalysts increase the total number of collisions.

items.prompt: Consider the reaction: NO(g) + O3(g) → NO2(g) + O2(g). If the concentration of NO is doubled while the concentration of O3 remains constant, the reaction rate doubles. If the concentration of both NO and O3 are doubled, the rate quadruples. Based on collision theory, what can be concluded about the molecular requirements for an effective collision in this reaction?
items.helper_text: Relate the change in concentration to the mathematical change in collision frequency.

options.label: A
options.text: The reaction is unimolecular, involving only the decomposition of NO.

options.label: B
options.text: An effective collision must involve a simultaneous encounter between one NO molecule and one O3 molecule.

options.label: C
options.text: The reaction rate is independent of the collision frequency between the two species.

options.label: D
options.text: The activation energy is halved when the concentration of both reactants is doubled.

items.explanation: The data shows the reaction is second-order overall (first-order with respect to both NO and O3). In collision theory, this implies that the rate-determining step requires a collision between the two different species. Doubling both increases the collision frequency by a factor of 2 x 2 = 4.

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that the rate dependency implies a bimolecular collision between the two reactants.
common_misconceptions: Assuming the reaction is zero-order because it is a single step.
Misinterpreting the rate change as a change in activation energy.

items.prompt: Two different gases, X and Y, react to form a product. For Gas X, the molecules are small and spherical. For Gas Y, the molecules are large, long-chain hydrocarbons. If both gases are at the same temperature and pressure, which statement regarding their reaction rates is most likely true based on collision theory?
items.helper_text: Think about the 'orientation factor' or 'steric factor' in collision theory.

options.label: A
options.text: Gas X will react faster because its molecules have a higher collision frequency due to smaller size.

options.label: B
options.text: Gas Y will react faster because large molecules have more surface area for collisions.

options.label: C
options.text: Gas X will react faster because the steric factor (orientation requirement) is likely less restrictive than for Gas Y.

options.label: D
options.text: The reaction rates will be identical because temperature and pressure are the same.

items.explanation: Collision theory states that for a collision to be effective, molecules must collide with correct orientation (the steric factor). Small, spherical molecules (Gas X) have many more successful orientation angles than large, complex molecules (Gas Y), which require very specific alignments to react. Thus, Gas X is likely to have a higher frequency of 'effective' collisions.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes that molecular complexity affects the probability of a successful orientation.
common_misconceptions: Focusing only on collision frequency and ignoring the orientation requirement.
Assuming larger size always leads to more collisions and thus a faster rate.

items.prompt: A student performs an experiment where the concentration of a reactant is increased by a factor of 3, but the observed reaction rate only increases by a factor of 1.5. Which of the following is the most scientifically sound explanation according to collision theory?
items.helper_text: Consider what happens when a reaction is not a single-step elementary process.

options.label: A
options.text: The reaction is zero-order, and the measurement error is high.

options.label: B
options.text: The increase in concentration did not result in a proportional increase in the frequency of effective collisions, possibly due to a complex mechanism.

options.label: C
options.text: The activation energy increased as the concentration of the reactant increased.

options.label: D
options.text: The temperature of the system must have decreased significantly during the reaction.

items.explanation: In simple elementary reactions, rate is directly proportional to concentration. However, in complex (multi-step) reactions, the rate is determined by the slowest step. If the reactant being increased is not involved in the rate-determining step, or if the reaction follows a fractional order, the rate increase will not be linear. This indicates the collision frequency of the specific rate-determining step did not scale 1:1 with the total concentration.

rubric.correct: The student identifies that non-linear rate changes suggest a complex reaction mechanism where not all collisions lead to the rate-determining step.
common_misconceptions: Assuming all reactions must follow integer-order kinetics.
Concluding that the experiment must be wrong rather than considering reaction mechanism.

items.prompt: An unknown element X has an atomic number of 26 and a mass number of 56. If this atom loses three electrons to form an ion X³⁺, what is the correct number of protons, neutrons, and electrons in the ion?
items.helper_text: Remember that the atomic number defines the element, while the charge only affects the electron count.

options.label: A
options.text: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons

options.label: B
options.text: 26 protons, 30 neutrons, 23 electrons

options.label: C
options.text: 23 protons, 30 neutrons, 26 electrons

options.label: D
options.text: 26 protons, 56 neutrons, 23 electrons

items.explanation: Protons are determined by the atomic number (26). Neutrons are calculated by Mass Number - Atomic Number (56 - 26 = 30). Electrons in a neutral atom equal protons (26), but since the ion has a 3+ charge, it has lost 3 electrons (26 - 3 = 23).

rubric.correct: The student correctly identifies that protons remain constant while electrons decrease due to the positive charge.
common_misconceptions: Subtracting the charge from the neutron count.
Confusing the mass number with the neutron count.

items.prompt: Two isotopes of an element, Isotope A and Isotope B, are analyzed. Isotope A has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Isotope B has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. Which of the following statements is true regarding these two isotopes?
items.helper_text: Focus on what changes between isotopes and what remains the same.

options.label: A
options.text: Isotope B has a higher chemical reactivity than Isotope A.

options.label: B
options.text: Isotope B has a higher atomic mass than Isotope A.

options.label: C
options.text: Isotope A and B have different chemical properties.

options.label: D
options.text: Isotope B has more electrons than Isotope A.

items.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons. Since Isotope B has 20 neutrons and Isotope A has 18, Isotope B is heavier. Chemical properties are determined by electrons/protons, which are identical here.

rubric.correct: The student recognizes that isotopes differ only in mass (neutrons) and not in chemical behavior.
common_misconceptions: Thinking isotopes have different chemical properties.
Assuming different neutron counts change the electron count.

items.prompt: An atom has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. If this atom gains one electron to achieve stability, what will be its new electron configuration and its resulting charge?
items.helper_text: Count the total electrons before and after the change.

options.label: A
options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, charge -1

options.label: B
options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, charge +1

options.label: C
options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, charge -1

options.label: D
options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵, charge -1

items.explanation: The original atom has 17 electrons. Adding one electron makes it 18 electrons. The configuration for 18 electrons is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. Because it gained a negative charge (electron), the ion charge is -1.

rubric.correct: The student correctly applies the Aufbau principle to the new electron count and identifies the correct ionic charge.
common_misconceptions: Confusing the addition of an electron with a positive charge.
Incorrectly writing the subshell sequence.

items.prompt: Given the following data: Element Y has 4 electron shells and its valence electrons are in the 4s and 3d subshells. If the subshells are filled according to the Aufbau principle, what is the most likely identity of element Y based on its position in the periodic table?
items.helper_text: Identify which block (s, p, d, or f) the valence electrons belong to.

options.label: A
options.text: An alkali metal in Period 4

options.label: B
options.text: A transition metal in Period 4

options.label: C
options.text: A noble gas in Period 4

options.label: D
options.text: An alkaline earth metal in Period 3

items.explanation: Elements that have electrons filling the 'd' subshell are classified as transition metals. Since the highest principal quantum number is 4, it belongs to Period 4.

rubric.correct: The student links subshell occupancy (d-block) to the specific group type (transition metals).
common_misconceptions: Confusing the period number with the group number.
Misidentifying d-block elements as main group elements.

items.prompt: In the context of the Bohr model versus the Quantum Mechanical model, which of the following statements best describes the fundamental difference in how electron location is described?
items.helper_text: Think about 'orbits' versus 'orbitals'.

options.label: A
options.text: Bohr describes electrons as particles in fixed circular orbits, while Quantum Mechanics describes them as waves in probabilistic orbitals.

options.label: B
options.text: Bohr describes electrons in clouds, while Quantum Mechanics describes them in specific energy levels.

options.label: C
options.text: Bohr uses probability density, while Quantum Mechanics uses exact mathematical paths.

options.label: D
options.text: There is no difference; both models treat electrons as having exact positions at all times.

items.explanation: The Bohr model proposes that electrons move in defined, predictable circular orbits. The Quantum Mechanical model (Schrödinger) uses wave functions to define orbitals, which are regions of high probability of finding an electron.

rubric.correct: The student distinguishes between the deterministic nature of Bohr's orbits and the probabilistic nature of quantum orbitals.
common_misconceptions: Equating orbits with orbitals.
Thinking the Bohr model is based on probability.

items.prompt: An atom of an element has a ground-state electron configuration ending in 3d¹⁰ 4s¹. If this atom is ionized to form a 2+ cation, what will be the electron configuration of the resulting ion?
items.helper_text: Always remove electrons from the highest principal quantum number (n) shell first.

options.label: A
options.text: [Ar] 3d⁹

options.label: B
options.text: [Ar] 3d¹⁰

options.label: C
options.text: [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁸

options.label: D
options.text: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁸

items.explanation: The neutral atom is Zinc (Zn), configuration [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ (Note: the prompt specifies 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ which is an excited state or specific instruction, but following standard ionization rules: electrons are removed from the highest principal quantum number shell first). For a 2+ ion, we remove 2 electrons. Removing from the 4s shell first (the highest n) results in [Ar] 3d¹⁰. Wait, if the prompt says 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, removing 2 electrons from that specific configuration: 1 from 4s and 1 from 3d results in 3d⁹. However, in standard chemistry, the 4s is removed first. If the configuration is [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰, 2+ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰. If we follow the prompt's specific configuration 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ and remove 2: one from 4s, one from 3d = 3d⁹. Let's re-evaluate the prompt logic. Standard Zn is 4s² 3d¹⁰. To make it 2+, we lose 4s² to get 3d¹⁰. If the prompt is a 'hard' question about the order of removal: electrons are removed from the highest n (4s) before the d-subshell.
